--- title: "Statistical modelling and machine learning" description: "The two share their data, their models and their fitting. They differ in aim: a statistical model estimates an effect, a machine-learning model predicts new cases. A straight line and a decision tree fitted to the same stations show the difference." order: 2 categories: [foundations] --- ## One toolbox, two aims Statistical modelling and machine learning are not two separate subjects. Both start from a table of measurements, both fit a model with parameters, and both fit it by making some measure of error as small as possible. Linear regression belongs to both. The difference is mostly one of aim. A statistical model is usually fitted to **estimate an effect**, such as the change in growth per degree of warming, and to report it with an interval. A machine-learning model is usually fitted to **predict** well for new cases it has not seen. That aim changes who chooses the shape of the relationship and how the model is checked. ::: {.diagram} ![Statistical modelling and machine learning compared. Methods sit on a scale from shapes you write down to shapes the algorithm finds; the middle of the scale is used by both.](img/statistics-and-ml.svg){fig-alt="At the top, a scale coloured from blue to orange runs from 'you write it down' to 'the algorithm finds it', with methods marked along it: t-test, ANOVA, linear regression, GLM, GAM, decision tree, random forest and neural network. A shaded patch over linear regression, GLM and GAM reads 'used by both'. Below it, a dashed band lists what the two share: data with measurements, a model with parameters, and fitting by making the error small. At the bottom, two boxes. Statistical modelling: the aim is to explain by estimating an effect, the result is a few numbers with intervals, it is checked by its assumptions, and the risk is that a wrong shape gives a wrong effect. Machine learning: the aim is to predict new cases the model has not seen, the result is a fitted model that turns new measurements into predictions, it is checked by the error on held-back data, and the risk is good predictions with no single effect."} ::: ## Both approaches on the same stations [The previous page](types-of-learning.qmd) ended with a puzzle: the linear regression found a temperature slope close to zero, yet presence depended strongly on temperature. Here the same question is answered both ways. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: First, a quarter of the stations are held back as a **test set**. Neither model sees them during fitting, so they show how each model does on new stations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) test <- testing(split) ``` ::: ### Statistical approach: a straight line The statistical approach writes down a straight line in each variable and reads the slopes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linear <- linear_reg() |> fit(abundance ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = train) tidy(linear, conf.int = TRUE) |> select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| conf.low| conf.high| p.value| |:-------------|----------:|-----------:|----------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 23.5429630| -26.8606947| 73.9466208| 0.3593359| |temperature_c | -0.0788643| -0.2315011| 0.0737726| 0.3106448| |salinity_psu | -0.4879045| -2.0046801| 1.0288710| 0.5277932| |depth_m | -0.0275390| -0.0416914| -0.0133866| 0.0001465|
::: ::: The temperature slope is again close to zero, and its interval spans zero. Read as usual, temperature has no detectable effect on abundance. ### Machine-learning approach: a decision tree The machine-learning approach uses a **decision tree**. It splits the stations in two at the threshold that best separates high counts from low ones, such as "temperature below 6.4 °C", then splits each half again. Here it stops after three rounds of splits and predicts the average count in each final group. Nobody writes down the shape; the splits find it. [Section 3](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) explains trees in full. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tree <- decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = 3) |> fit(abundance ~ temperature_c + salinity_psu + depth_m, data = train) ``` ::: ### A straight line misses a temperature optimum @fig-shapes shows what each model predicts across the range of temperature, with salinity and depth held at their typical values. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid <- tibble( temperature_c = seq(min(survey$temperature_c), max(survey$temperature_c), by = 0.05), salinity_psu = median(train$salinity_psu), depth_m = median(train$depth_m) ) curves <- bind_rows( mutate(grid, model = "Linear regression", .pred = predict(linear, grid)$.pred), mutate(grid, model = "Decision tree", .pred = predict(tree, grid)$.pred) ) ggplot(train, aes(temperature_c, abundance)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = .pred, colour = model), linewidth = 1.2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Linear regression" = ml_palette[["blue"]], "Decision tree" = ml_palette[["orange"]])) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 15)) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Abundance (animals per station)", colour = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Predicted abundance against temperature, with salinity and depth held at their medians. The straight line is nearly flat; the tree finds low counts in cold and warm water and the most animals in between.](what-is-machine-learning_files/figure-html/fig-shapes-1.png){#fig-shapes fig-alt='Scatter of abundance against temperature for the training stations, with counts highest between about 6 and 11 degrees. A nearly flat straight line runs through the points. A stepped line, the tree, sits low below 6.4 degrees, rises to its highest level between 6.4 and 11.1 degrees, and drops again above.' width=1400} ::: ::: The species does best in middling water and thins out in colder and warmer water. A straight line through a hump is flat, so the linear model reports no effect. The tree was never asked for a slope, so the hump costs it nothing. On the test set it predicts a little better: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bind_rows( augment(linear, test) |> rmse(abundance, .pred) |> mutate(model = "Linear regression"), augment(tree, test) |> rmse(abundance, .pred) |> mutate(model = "Decision tree") ) |> select(model, test_rmse = .estimate) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | test_rmse| |:-----------------|---------:| |Linear regression | 4.585037| |Decision tree | 4.392486|
::: ::: `test_rmse` is the root mean squared error on the test stations: square each prediction error, average them, and take the square root. It is in animals per station, so a value of 2 means predictions for new stations are usually off by about 2 animals, in either direction. Lower is better. Neither model is simply better. The tree found the shape but gives no single number for "the effect of temperature". The linear model gives that number, but the number is wrong because the shape was wrong. A statistician would bend the line instead, which [the next page](prediction-and-explanation.qmd) does. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Statistical modelling and machine learning share their data, their models and their fitting. Linear regression belongs to both. - They differ in aim: a statistical model estimates an effect, a machine-learning model predicts new cases. - In a statistical model you choose the shape of the relationship; in most machine-learning methods the algorithm finds it. - A flat, non-significant slope can mean "no relationship" or "a relationship the model cannot draw". The output looks the same. - Machine-learning models are checked on a test set: stations held back from fitting. ::: ## Try it yourself Add a squared temperature term to the linear model (`abundance ~ temperature_c + I(temperature_c^2) + salinity_psu + depth_m`). Is the temperature effect detectable now, and how does the test error compare with the tree's?
